source.version: Journal version of record: AI (MDPI) 2025, 6, 247, https://doi.org/10.3390/ai6100247; received 20 July 2025, revised 30 August 2025, accepted 16 September 2025, published 1 October 2025 (p. 1). retrieval.json lists this file as the latest version.
source.title_on_document: Creativeable: Leveraging AI for Personalized Creativity Enhancement

supplement.holds: Text S1 (prompt that generated the SWT word triplets), Text S2 (prompt for feedback and difficulty adjustment), Text S3 (prompt that rated story creativity), Text S4 (reflection questions after each story), Table S1 (word triplets with semantic distance and difficulty ratings), Table S2 (examples of creativity improvement suggestions). The listing names no outcome statistics or standard errors. All reported creativity statistics are in the main text. Data and code are on OSF (p. 25).

paper_design_summary: Prolific participants, recruited in four batches with one batch per condition (385 analyzed), wrote five short stories (60-80 words, three given words per story) under one of four conditions that cross GPT-4 feedback after each story (yes/no) with GPT-4-adjusted task difficulty (yes/no). NF/CL, with neither, is the paper's control. Before and after training, every participant did two Alternative Uses Task items without AI (originality scored by OCSAI, plus fluency) and an animal semantic fluency control task, and GPT-4 rated the creativity of every training story.

studies.label: Creativeable training experiment (four batch-recruited conditions, story writing; AUT before and after)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Training condition (F/VL, F/CL, NF/VL, NF/CL): GPT-4 feedback and an improvement suggestion after each story (yes/no) crossed with GPT-4-adjusted task difficulty (yes/no). Condition followed recruitment batch, one batch per condition, so everyone in a batch received the same condition. The paper never says that people were randomly assigned.
assignment.quote: Recruitment was conducted in four separate batches, each corresponding to one of the study’s experimental conditions, to ensure smooth operation of the study platform.
assignment.locator: p. 6, Section 2.1 Participants; p. 23, Section 4.5 Limitations (batch timing named as a concern); p. 5, Section 1.5 (between-subject design)

arms.name: F/VL
arms.description: Feedback with varying difficulty: after each round the GPT-4 'creativity trainer' gives two-sentence general feedback on the story and one suggestion for improving creativity, and raises, keeps, or lowers the next triplet's difficulty based on performance and self-reported fatigue.

arms.name: F/CL
arms.description: Feedback with constant difficulty: the same GPT-4 feedback and suggestions as F/VL; difficulty stays at medium-easy for all five rounds.

arms.name: NF/VL
arms.description: No feedback, varying difficulty: no feedback is shown; the GPT-4 trainer adjusts the next triplet's difficulty after each round based on performance and fatigue. Participants see no AI-generated text.

arms.name: NF/CL
arms.description: The paper's control condition: no feedback and no difficulty adjustment; five rounds at constant medium-easy difficulty. Participants have no AI interaction; GPT-4 rated their stories only during data processing.

participants.exclusions: Participants were excluded if they did not complete the study, gave overly brief responses, or completed the tasks unusually quickly (p. 6). The number excluded and the number recruited before exclusions are not stated. The 385 people the paper calls 'included in the study' are the people analyzed. Table 1 arm counts (97, 98, 93, 97) sum to 385, and the analysis df (F(3, 381), pp. 13-16) match.
participants.who: Prolific participants, native English speakers aged 18-45 with at least 12 years of formal education, paid £9 per hour; mean age 28.8 to 31.7 by arm (Table 1). Recruitment targeted about 100 per condition.
participants.quote: A total of 385 participants were included in the study, recruited via the crowdsourcing platform Prolific.
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 2.1 and Table 1 (N: F/VL 97, F/CL 98, NF/VL 93, NF/CL 97)

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 via API (the 'creativity trainer'). GPT-4 also rated story creativity during data processing, and OCSAI (a prompted GPT instance) scored AUT originality.
ai_tool.how_used: In F/VL and F/CL, after each submitted story a summary page showed two-sentence general feedback on that story and one suggestion for improving creativity or brainstorming in the next round (p. 9, Section 2.2.7; p. 7, Figure 1). The procedure describes no revision of a submitted story, each round uses a new triplet, and the AI wrote no story content. In F/VL and NF/VL, GPT-4 also chose whether to raise, keep, or lower the next triplet's difficulty, based on performance and reported fatigue (p. 9, Section 2.2.6). In NF/VL this is the AI's only role. The AI was not part of the pre- and post-training AUT or the semantic fluency task. Because the trainer comments on the person's own submitted story, 'refinement' partly fits, but no draft is revised.

task.description: Training: Story Writing Task, five rounds; each round a short story of about three to four sentences (60-80 words) that uses all three given words. GPT generated triplets with increasing semantic distance, and 17 crowd raters' difficulty ratings sorted them into four levels (E, ME, MH, H); every participant started at medium-easy. Assessment before and after training (the outcome task): Alternative Uses Task, two items each time, 2 minutes per item, plus an animal semantic fluency task (2 minutes) as a non-creative control.
task.duration: Whole study about 50 minutes on average (p. 10, Section 2.5); 2 minutes per AUT item and 2 minutes for the semantic fluency task (p. 10)

outcomes.name: Post-training AUT originality (OCSAI score, 1-5)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: OCSAI (online scoring platform using a prompted GPT instance) scores the originality of each use from 1 to 5; scores are averaged within each item, then across the two post-training items, and the pre-training score is built the same way (p. 10, Section 2.3). The paper analyzes it as post-training scores (one-way ANOVA, Tukey HSD), pre/post change (mixed-design ANOVA, within-arm t-tests), and percent improvement from pre to post (one-way ANOVA, Tukey HSD). These are variants of one outcome.
outcomes.delay: Same session, right after the five training rounds

outcomes.name: Post-training AUT fluency (number of uses)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of uses per AUT item, averaged over the two items in each phase, with the same averaging as originality (p. 10, Section 2.3).
outcomes.delay: Same session, right after the five training rounds

contrasts.reported: Time (pre vs post) x condition mixed-design ANOVA on the number of AUT responses: time F(1, 381) = 0.04, p = 0.90, η² = 0.0; time x condition F(3, 381) = 1.53, p = 0.2, η² = 0.01. No condition main effect or pairwise test is printed. Arm means with 95% CIs appear only in Figure 4.

outcomes.name: GPT-4-rated creativity of the training stories (1-5), rounds 1-5
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: During data processing GPT-4, prompted as a creative writing expert, rated each story's creativity from 1 to 5 (how imaginative, surprising, and original the characters and plot were, and how creatively the three words were integrated); each story was rated five times and the score is the mean (pp. 8-9, Section 2.2.5). Analyzed as a condition x round mixed-design ANOVA, with within-arm repeated-measures ANOVAs and round-to-round t-tests. Each participant wrote one story per round, so the rows are stories nested in participants, and the tests use participant degrees of freedom. Feedback arrives only after each story is submitted, so round 1 precedes any feedback. The VL arms moved to harder triplets in later rounds, so arm levels mix triplet difficulty with the treatment.

contrasts.reported: Condition x round mixed-design ANOVA: condition F(3, 381) = 29.48, p < 0.001, η² = 0.155; round F(4, 1524) = 10.21, p < 0.001, η² = 0.026; condition x round F(12, 1524) = 2.01, p = 0.02, η² = 0.016. No arm means pooled over rounds, no NF-arm round means, and no between-arm post hoc tests are printed, so the direction of the condition effect is not stated. Within arm: F/VL F(4, 384) = 3.32, p = 0.01, η² = 0.018, round 1 M = 2.7 (SD = 0.6) to round 3 M = 2.98 (SD = 0.79), t(96) = 3.12, p = 0.02, Cohen’s d = 0.38; F/CL F(4, 388) = 12.14, p < 0.001, η² = 0.058, round 1 M = 3.03 (SD = 0.66) to round 3 M = 3.49 (SD = 0.69), t(97) = 5.52, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 0.43, and to round 5 M = 3.44 (SD = 0.75), t(97) = 4.97, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 0.57; NF arms: no significant change across rounds (all p’s > 0.05). Scores across all conditions 'fluctuated between approximately 2.5 and 3.6'.

eligibility.reason: Conditions were filled by four separate recruitment batches, one per condition (p. 6, Section 2.1; p. 23, Section 4.5), and the paper never states random assignment, so people were not randomly assigned to AI and criterion 1 fails (quasi_people, folded into observational context). 385 people were analyzed (97, 98, 93, 97; p. 6, Table 1), well above 50. Outcomes are scored on the output: OCSAI originality and the fluency count of AUT uses produced after the AI was removed (after_ai, p. 10), and GPT-4 ratings of the training stories (with_ai, pp. 8-9).

one_line_finding: In four batch-recruited (non-random) conditions, AUT originality scored without AI rose from pre to post training in every arm, no GPT-4 arm differed significantly from the no-AI control after training (post means F/CL 2.81, F/VL 2.71, NF/VL 2.89 vs NF/CL 2.84), and F/VL scored below NF/VL (∆M = 0.175, SE = 0.06, p = 0.014, d = 0.41) and improved less than F/CL (4.82 vs 11.6 percent, mean difference 6.77, SE = 2.25, p = 0.015) (pp. 13-14, Section 3.2.1).
open_questions: The paper says only that each recruitment batch corresponded to one condition. It does not say how batches were ordered or timed, or how conditions were matched to batches. Everyone in a batch received the same condition, so people were not individually randomized either way.

Scope: in the feedback arms GPT-4 comments on the participant's submitted story and suggests a strategy for the next round but writes no content (coded coach). In NF/VL, GPT-4 only chooses the next triplet's difficulty and participants see no AI text, yet the arm is coded generative_ai, as both screeners did. Review 1 may want to decide whether these count as generative-AI assistance.
For the GPT-4 story ratings (S1-O3), AI availability is coded mixed: feedback came between rounds, not while writing, round 1 preceded any feedback, and NF/CL had no AI.

The direction of the large condition effect on GPT-4 story ratings (F(3, 381) = 29.48) is not printed. Round-1 scores already differ between F/VL (2.7) and F/CL (3.03) before any feedback, which may reflect batch differences, and the VL arms wrote to harder triplets.
How many participants were excluded, and from which arms? The paper gives only the exclusion rules (p. 6).
notes: Outcomes not listed (form-spec rule 7): (1) the animal semantic fluency task, which the paper uses as a non-creative control (time F(1, 381) = 0.40, p = 0.52, η² = 0.001; time x condition F(3, 381) = 0.29, p = 0.83, η² = 0.002; condition F(3, 381) = 5.0, p = 0.01, η² = 0.04; means only in Figure 5; p. 15); (2) participants' self-rated creativity of each story (self_report, not scored on the output; round F(4, 1524) = 6.34, p < 0.001, η² = 0.16; condition F(3, 381) = 3.38, p = 0.018, η² = 0.03; interaction F(12, 1524) = 0.16, p = 0.99, η² = 0.001; p. 16); (3) perceived task difficulty, self-reported fatigue, and usefulness ratings of the AI suggestions (Figure 7), all self-reports (pp. 9-11, 19). Overall AUT originality: pre M = 2.6 (SD = 0.36), post M = 2.81 (SD = 0.4), time F(1, 381) = 108.76, p < 0.001, η² = 0.22; condition F(3, 381) = 2.5, p = 0.06, η² = 0.019; time x condition F(3, 381) = 2.74, p = 0.043, η² = 0.021; pre-training one-way ANOVA F(3, 381) = 1.6, p = 0.18, η² = 0.012 (p. 13). Within-arm pre/post tests: F/VL t(96) = 2.75, d = 0.28; F/CL t(97) = 6.38, d = 0.65; NF/VL t(92) = 5.94, d = 0.58; NF/CL t(96) = 5.97, d = 0.59; all printed with p < 0.001 (pp. 13-14). Possible reporting errors to check at extraction (values above are recorded as printed): the post-training one-way ANOVA F(3, 381) = 3.34 is printed with p = 0.002, but that F on those df gives p near 0.02 (p. 13); F/VL pre/post t(96) = 2.75 is printed with p < 0.001, but that t gives p near 0.007 (p. 13); the fatigue interaction F(12, 1524) = 1.37 is printed with p = 0.017 and called not significant, and that F gives p near 0.17 (p. 11); the semantic fluency condition effect F(3, 381) = 5.0 is printed with p = 0.01, and that F gives p near 0.002 (p. 15); the AUT fluency time effect F(1, 381) = 0.04 is printed with p = 0.90, and that F gives p near 0.84 (p. 14); Table 1 M/F counts sum to 96 for F/VL and NF/CL while N = 97 (p. 6); Section 2.1 says chi-squared tests found no age difference across groups, while Section 4.5 reports a marginal age difference (p = 0.05, η² = 0.02) (pp. 6, 23); the Figure 3 caption says '(left; AUT originality)' but the figure has one panel (p. 14); Section 3.2.2 (p. 16) and Section 4.5 (p. 24) cite Figure 4 for the GPT-4 story scores, but Figure 4 shows AUT fluency, and no figure or table gives arm-level story scores. The Acknowledgments say the authors used GPT-4 to develop the tool, analyze responses, and provide real-time feedback (p. 25). open_items.item: Batch order and timing (open question 1): each of the four recruitment batches corresponded to one condition (p. 6, Section 2.1), and Section 4.5 names 'potential concerns about temporal differences in participant recruitment' (p. 23), but the paper gives no batch order, dates, or rule for matching conditions to batches. Criterion 1 fails under any answer, because everyone in a batch received the same condition and no person was randomly assigned. The answer matters only for describing this observational context record.

Scope of the AI arms (open question 2): the feedback arms are coded coach (GPT-4 comments on the submitted story and suggests one strategy, and writes no story content), and NF/VL is coded generative_ai although GPT-4 only chooses the next triplet's difficulty and participants see no AI text. This is a codebook decision for Review 1. It does not change eligibility, because criterion 1 fails on assignment for every arm.

AI availability for the GPT-4 story ratings (open question 3): S1-O3 is coded mixed, because feedback came between rounds and not during writing, round 1 preceded any feedback, and NF/CL had no AI. This is a coding choice for the with_ai record. Criterion 3 holds either way: the AUT originality and fluency scores (p. 10) and the story ratings (pp. 8-9) are all scored on the output.

Direction of the condition effect on the GPT-4 story ratings (open question 4): F(3, 381) = 29.48 is printed without arm means pooled over rounds, NF-arm round means, or between-arm post hoc tests (p. 16), and round-1 means already differ between F/VL (2.7) and F/CL (3.03) before any feedback. The posted data and code (https://osf.io/5kxv8/) would give arm means by round. This bears on extraction, not on eligibility.

Exclusions (open question 5): the paper states the exclusion rules but not the number recruited, the number excluded, or their arms (p. 6). Criterion 2 is met under any answer: 385 people were analyzed (p. 6, Table 1), and the between-arm df F(3, 381) match.

Printed p-values that do not fit their test statistics (listed in notes): post-training one-way ANOVA F(3, 381) = 3.34 with p = 0.002 (p. 13); F/VL pre/post t(96) = 2.75 with p < 0.001 (p. 13); fatigue interaction F(12, 1524) = 1.37 with p = 0.017 (p. 11); semantic fluency condition effect F(3, 381) = 5.0 with p = 0.01 (p. 15); AUT fluency time effect F(1, 381) = 0.04 with p = 0.90 (p. 14). The posted data and code would show which number is wrong. None bears on eligibility.
